catalog_quote: 5.2.5 Stress and intonation. Given the different definitions of “stress” in the literature, I clarify my use of the term as “the putative phonetic property” of “greater prominence” (Himmelmann & Ladd 2008:248), whereby such prominence can potentially be phonetically realized as “some combination of increased pitch, length and loudness” (Ladefoged (2003:90). Phrasal stress usually occurs on the penultimate syllable in declarative sentences. Detailed instrumental study of stress and intonation in PLMRT is a matter I reserve for future study. ... [p.135] The C-final citation form is the product of (1) deletion of that final vowel, and (2) vowel-lengthening of monosyllabic forms as a result of stress placement at the phrasal level, which applies in many Micronesian languages (Rehg 1984).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both the deciding sentence (sec. 5.2.5, printed p.117 / p.131) and the supporting sec. 5.4 remark (p.135) are verbatim in the extracted text we hold of Odango 2015 at the stated lines and form-feed count. (2) Deciding source is a 2015 fieldwork dissertation with a dedicated phonology chapter by the only linguist to have described Mortlockese in modern times; Glottolog's entire descriptive bibliography is an 1899 14-pp sketch and Odango's own 2014 syntax article, and web searches found no JIPA illustration, phonology article, or other thesis on Mortlockese prosody. The source itself says word-level/instrumental stress study is deferred, so 'phrasal, penultimate in declaratives, no word-stress rule' is a faithful and complete reading. (3) Nothing language-specific is missing; the one works still to obtain (Rehg 1993, print-only) is family-level context whose summary in the downloaded Him

sources.quote: Does not name Mortlockese. 'Stress is often described impressionistically ... without properly distinguishing word-based and phrase-based prominence ... Furthermore, Rehg (1993) claims that the major pitch excursions occurring on the penultimate syllable do not necessarily correlate with stress in Micronesian languages.'

tone.quote: Man hört nun in der Mortlock-Mundart folgende Laute: a) Vokale. ... au wie unser au, der Ton ruht aber mehr auf dem ä. ... b) Konsonanten. ... Der Einfachheit halber sind nur die Längebezeichnungen der Vokale durch einen Strich wiedergegeben, Kürzebezeichnungen fortgelassen worden. ... [p.178] ke se mwö^en lüntö? Willst du nicht zurückkommen? Die Frage ist nur durch den Ton oder Fragewörter zu erkennen.
tone.locator: pp.166-167, section 'Die Laute der Sprache und ihre schriftliche Wiedergabe' (vowel list incl. the au remark on p.166; consonants and the length-mark sentence on p.167); p.178, section 'Satzbau' (interrogative sentences), for 'Die Frage ist nur durch den Ton oder Fragewoerter zu erkennen'.
tone.translation: In the Mortlock dialect one hears the following sounds: a) Vowels. ... au like our au, but the emphasis rests more on the a. ... b) Consonants. ... For simplicity only the length marks of the vowels are given, by a stroke; shortness marks have been omitted. ... [p.178] ke se mwoshen lunto? Won't you come back? The question is recognisable only by the tone (intonation) or by question words.
